      Abstract
Fog of War chess is a popular variant of classical chess, in which both players have only partial
information about the position of the opponent’s pieces. This study provides the first theoretical
analysis of endgames in Fog of War chess. In particular, we analyze the setups king and queen versus
king, king and rook versus king, and king and two rooks versus king. We show that a king and
queen can always guarantee a win against a lone king. In contrast to classical chess, a king and a
rook cannot guarantee a win against a lone king. However, adding one more rook guarantees a win.

 1      Introduction
Fog of War chess, also known as Dark chess, is a variant of the popular board game chess,
where each player can only see the squares to which their pieces can legally move. The game
was invented by Jens Bæk Nielsen and Torben Osted in 1989 [9] and is based on Kriegspiel,
which is the first variant of chess with limited information, introduced in 1899 [10].
    The aspect of imperfect information adds uncertainty to the game, as players must
make decisions based on incomplete information about their opponent’s pieces and positions.
Recently, in June 2025, the design of an AI-strategy is described, also first theoretical
thoughts about the scenario of one king versus another king are mentioned [10]. Even in the
wider social and cultural context, Fog of War chess is recognized: Notably, on the popular
chess website chess.com, tens of thousands of players actively play Fog of War chess, making
it one of the most popular chess variants [2]. World-class players such as Hikaru Nakamura
are known for playing the variant [8], and it has also gained a lot of traction online with
millions of views [6].
    Also, other games for which imperfect information plays an important role have already
been studied in the past, including minesweeper [7], tetris [5], or other video games [3].
    In this article, we will study endgames in Fog of War chess from a theoretical perspective:
    The main contribution therefore, is three different endgames in Fog of War chess, where
we show which combination of pieces can guarantee a win against a lone king.
    First, we will introduce the rules of Fog of War chess, including some terminology.
    In the three following sections, we analyze which pieces are sufficient to guarantee a win
against a lone king, given the opponent’s initial king position, but without knowledge of
their subsequent moves. We will first show that a king and queen can always guarantee a
win. After that, we consider the setup king and rook versus a king. We will show that there
are starting positions where the player with the rook cannot guarantee a win. This is in
contrast to classical chess, where a king and rook can always win against a lone king, given
he starts and plays optimally [4]. Lastly, we consider the setup king and two rooks versus a
king. We will show that the player with the two rooks can guarantee a win.
    We conclude this article with some open questions.

       1.1     Rules
       The rules of Fog of War chess are similar to those of classical chess [10]. The chess pieces
       move as in classical chess. The imperfect information changes the game as follows:
         The players observe only the squares their pieces can legally move to, after each move.
         There is no check or checkmate; a player wins by taking the opponent’s king. Thus,
             if one player moves into a check with its king, then this is legal, but immediately loses
             the game, as there is no better move for the opponent than taking the opponent’s king.
             there is no stalemate, particularly if one player can only move to a square which is
             attacked by the opponent, and it is his turn, he loses.
         A draw does not have to be claimed. In particular, a threefold repetition and the draw
          after 50 moves without a pawn move or capture must be enforced by the game host.
         There are additional rules for pawns:
             If a pawn’s forward move is blocked by a piece, then it cannot observe that piece. But
             of course, he then knows that there is an opponent’s piece in front of him.
             En passant is allowed; therefore, if a pawn can do so, the opponent’s pawn is visible.

          Within this study, the pawn rules are not relevant; furthermore, we ignore the draw rules.
          If White has a winning strategy, he must win regardless of how the Black king moves. As
       the Black king might be lucky and always guess the right move, we may assume that Black
       knows the board and can play adversarial.

       1.2     Notation
       We use the classic chess notation to refer to squares on the board as depicted in figure 1.
           The file of the chessboard is its column (A − H), while the rank is its row (1 − 8) [1]. We
       call a square an edge- or a corner square, when it is at the edge (resp. corner) of the board.
       Without loss of generality, we will present strategies for White for the rest of this article.
       With, e.g., (A–C, 1–3), we denote the set of all squares on the rectangle between A1 and C3.
       A configuration is the position of all pieces on the board.

        2      Queen and King vs. King
       In classical chess, a player with a queen and a king can always force a win against a lone
       king [4]. In this section, we will show that this is also possible in Fog of War Chess:
M. Gehnen and J. Stannat                                                                              21:3


   We will present a strategy for White that guarantees a win for any given configuration
and regardless of Black’s moves. Therefore, we need to show that White’s strategy holds for
any move Black performs. This may lead to multiple possible positions of the Black king, of
which White does not know where exactly Black is.
   The winning strategy for White proceeds in two stages:
1. White moves its king onto a corner square (A1, H1, A8, or H8) and places the queen on
   an adjacent square. So if the white king is on A1, then the queen is placed on either A2,
   B2, or B1. We call this a corner configuration.
2. White gradually reduces the set of squares available for the opponent’s king until capture
   becomes inevitable. This is done by pushing the opponent’s king towards an edge.


2.1    Preparing Observations
We begin with a number of observations laying the ground for the winning strategy.
    First, we note that whenever the opponent’s king can be captured, White should do so.
This implies that as long as the White king or queen are not moved, they cannot be captured
in the next round, as they would have been able to capture the Black king before.
    Secondly, the queen can always move around their own king without risk of losing it.

▶ Lemma 1. If the queen is adjacent to her own king, the queen can reach any other square
adjacent to the white king. If the queen gets captured, White wins immediately.

Proof. Whenever the queen moves to a square adjacent to their own king, she cannot be
captured. If Blacks king were to capture her, then he has moved his king to a place adjacent
to the White king. As the next move is from White, he will capture the Black king with his
own king and therefore win. It is also easy to see that White needs at most two moves to
move its queen from one square adjacent to their king to another square.                  ◀


2.2    Stage 1: Achieving the corner configuration
Our goal is to reach the corner configuration in finitely many moves.
   The objective of moving the White king to a corner and the queen to an adjacent square
can be divided into different cases: If the white king is initially on one of the central squares
(D4, D5, E4, or E5), then the first step is to move him out of the center. Once the white
king leaves the center, or if he initially does not start on a square in the center, we move
the queen to an adjacent square. Finally, we coordinate whites figures to reach the corner
configuration.
   We begin by proving the last step: if the white king is not in the middle of the board and
the queen is located on an adjacent square, then the corner configuration can be reached.

▶ Lemma 2. The White player has a king and a queen. The Black player only has a king.
It is White’s turn to move. The Black king can be on any square of the board.
    Suppose the White king is not on one of the central squares D4, D5, E4, or E5, and the
White queen is on a square adjacent to her king. Then either
   the corner configuration can be reached in finitely many moves, or
   White wins.

▶ Lemma 3 (Ensuring a Safe Way). Let the White king be on one of the central squares
{D4, D5, E4, E5}, White controls a queen, and the sole remaining Black piece is a king
(whose initial position is known). It is White’s turn to move.
   Without loss of generality, White can either place its king on D5 while ensuring that
Black’s king is on (D–H, 1–5) before the next move of White, or win.

Proof. Suppose the White king is on square D5 by symmetry.
   If the Black king is not already in (D–H, 1–5), we can move our king and achieve our
desired configuration up to symmetry:
   If the Black king is anywhere on the squares (E–H, 6–8), then
       If the Black king is on E6, then take him.
       Otherwise: try to move the White king to D4 if not blocked by the queen.
       ∗ If the queen is on D4, then move the king to C4: the king is not in the center, and
           the queen is adjacent to him, letting us invoke Lemma 2.
       ∗ Otherwise: move the White king to D4. It is Black’s turn to move. If he moves,
           then he can only move to any square from (D–H, 5–8). Rotating the board yields
           the desired result.
   If the Black king is on the squares (A–C, 1–4), this is analogous to the previous case.
   If the Black king is on the squares (A–D, 5–8), then we can use a similar strategy.
       If the Black king can be taken, White does so.
       Otherwise: try to move the White king to E4 if not blocked by the queen.
       ∗ If the queen is on that square, first move to E5 and then to F 4, which can be done
          without a risk of capture. Again, we can continue with Lemma 2.
       ∗ Otherwise: move the king to E4, then it is Black’s turn. If he moves, then he can
           only safely move to any square from (A–E, 4–8) except the squares adjacent to the
          White king. Rotate the board by 180 degrees, and we have reached the goal.       ◀

   Given such a configuration, we can safely move the king to any square up-left of the
board, as the Black king cannot outpace the White king.

   Then White can either reach the corner configuration or win.

Proof. We now want to move our king, such that the queen can move to an adjacent square
of the king on the next move without the risk of being captured. To ensure this, we make a
case distinction based on the position of the White queen.

▶ Corollary 6. Starting from any position in which White controls a king and queen and
moves first against a lone Black king, and White knows the Black king’s initial position, it is
always possible (in finitely many moves) to reach the corner configuration or to win.

    Note that the knowledge of Blacks initial position is crucial: even if Whites figures are
adjacent to each other, White will not be able to safely move its own king from the center to
a corner (as in Lemma 4). If White starts already in a corner configuration, knowing the
initial position of Black is not necessary.

2.3    Stage 2: Push the Black king to the edge, line by line
We now show that it is possible to systematically reduce the cardinality of the set of squares
available to the lone Black king. The reduction proceeds line by line (either rank or file),
beginning with line 1 and 2. For all proofs in this part, we can assume that White starts, as
black can start on an arbitrary position (within the given restrictions).

▶ Lemma 7. White controls a king and a queen in a corner configuration, Black has a king.
   Then Black can be restricted to a 6 × 8 area, or White wins.

Proof. Let the White king be on A1 and the queen on A2. Use the following strategy:
1. Move the queen one square to the right (first to B2). She is protected by the White king,
   so if she is taken, White wins.
2. Move the White king to the right. This move is safe as all adjacent positions are visible
   due to the queen on the position above.
3. Repeat steps (1.), (2.) until the queen reaches H2.
This procedure works for the following reasons:
   If the Black king is on line 2, (A–H, 2), then the queen can take him and White wins.
   If the Black king is on line 1, (A–H, 1), then the queen will discover him. If the Black
   king moves further to the right, at some point, he is stuck and can be taken by the queen.
   If he takes the queen, then the White king takes and White wins.
   Afterwards, the Black king is not on the first or second rank, namely (A–H, 1–2).              ◀

       be located on an arbitrary position within (A–H, 3–8).
           First, we move the queen and the king one step at a time to the right, until the queen
       sees the Black king. If the queen sees the Black king, the king can be forced upwards:

       ▶ Lemma 8. Let the White player have a king and a queen, and the Black player only a
       king. The White queen is adjacent to her own king. The Black king is located in a 6 × 8 area,
       which is restricted by the queen.
           Then White can either win the game or force the Black king upwards until restricting
       him to a 3 × 8 square field.

       We show the procedure from rank 5 and above to 6 and above; the other cases are identical.

       Proof. Suppose that the White queen is located on position A4 and her king is on B3, and
       the Black king is located on an arbitrary square (A–H, 5–8). Other configurations are similar.
          The strategy proceeds in two phases:
          First, we move the queen and the king to the right, one step at a time, until the queen
          sees the Black king above her.
          Once the queen sees the Black king, we force him upwards, ultimately restricting him to
          a 3 × 8 area, namely (A–H, 6–8).

          It is White’s turn to move. White follows the strategy below:
       1. If White sees the Black king, then he captures immediately.
       2. Otherwise, if the Black king is unseen, White follows a fixed sequence of moves as
          illustrated in Figure 7.
       3. If for i = 0, i = 2 or i = 4 we see the Black king in the same file as the queen, we move
          the king diagonally up-right, then follow with the queen one square up.
       4. If for i = 5 we see the Black king in the same file as the queen, we move the king
          diagonally up-left, then follow with the queen one square up.

       Correctness. We now prove the reduction of the Black king’s possible positions:
          In the trivial cases (Black king is directly visible, or captures the queen), White either
          wins by immediate capture or recaptures with the king (the queen is always protected).

        Finally, we consider the endgame of a king and two rooks against a king. As before, let White
        have a king and two rooks, and Black only a king. White starts and knows the starting
        position of Black. We prove that for any starting position of the Black and White figures,
        there exists a winning strategy for White. Also in classical chess, this is a win for White [4].
           The strategy consists of three stages, organized in three lemmas below. In the first stage,
        we will prove that White can move the two rooks on one rank/file while ensuring that the
        own king is not on it as well. Secondly, we will show that we can move the White king into
        one corner and the two rooks are adjacent to him. And lastly, we will prove that the two
        rooks and the king can force a checkmate from the edge position.

        and their own king is not on either the same rank or file.

         5     Final Comments and Open Questions
        We showed that in Fog of War chess, given that one player has a king and queen and plays
        against a lone king, he can always guarantee a win. In contrast to classical chess, if one
        player has a king and a rook, then he cannot guarantee a win against a player with a lone
        king. However, adding one more rook for the player with the rook guarantees a win for him.
            In Fog of War chess, there exist many more open questions concerning endgames:
            First and foremost, endgames using knights, bishops, or a combination of several pieces
        are yet to be answered. As in classical chess, endgames can also occur where the opponent
        has not just the king, but also a few more own pieces available.
            Another relevant question is to minimize the number of moves one player needs to make
        to ensure a win. We suspect that our strategy for king and queen versus king cannot be
        performed within 50 moves, which might be relevant when one plays with a fifty-move rule.
        Potentially, another strategy could guarantee a win faster and within 50 moves. Our strategy
        for king and two rooks versus king however, should work within 50 moves.
            We also ignore the draw rule for move repetition. While our studied strategies do not
        require repeating moves, there might be other endgames in Fog of War chess where this
        aspect becomes crucial (as, e.g., the algorithm might need to repeat its moves for restricting
        the space for opponents pieces).
            Finally, it is worth mentioning that also other variants with limited knowledge about the
        board than the classical Fog of War variant might yield interesting results.
            In conclusion, Fog of War chess presents a rich field for theoretical exploration, with
        many open questions and potential for further research.
            We hope that our work contributes to the understanding of endgames in Fog of War chess
        and opens up avenues for future research in this intriguing variant of chess.
